questions.q: Why did the men of Israel say that one of their tribes might not exist anymore?
questions.a: The men of Israel worried that the Benjaminite tribe would no longer exist since they had promised to not allow their daughters to marry a Benjaminite so the remaining men would not have women to marry.

questions.q: Who would certainly be put to death?
questions.a: Anyone who did not come when they met with Yahweh at Mizpah would certainly be put to death.

questions.q: Which of the cities did not come to meet with Yahweh at Mizpah?
questions.a: No one from the city of Jabesh Gilead had come to meet with Yahweh at Mizpah.

questions.q: Who did the men take from those living in Jabesh Gilead?
questions.a: The men took 400 young women who had never slept with a man from those living in Jabesh Gilead.

questions.q: What was the problem when the Benjaminites were given the women of Jabesh Gilead?
questions.a: When the Benjaminites were given the women of Jabesh Gilead, there were not enough women for all of them to marry.
Shiloh was north of Bethel, east of the road that went up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah.

questions.q: When were the Benjaminites to each rush out of the vineyards and grab a wife from the young women of Shiloh?
questions.a: When the young women from Shiloh came out to dance, each Benjaminite was to rush out of the vineyards and grab a young woman as his wife.

questions.q: Why would the men of Shiloh not be guilty of breaking their oath?
questions.a: The men of Shiloh were told that they had not broken their oath since they had not given their daughters to the Benjaminites as wives but instead, the young women had been stolen.

questions.q: How did everyone live in those days when Israel had no king?
questions.a: Everyone did what he thought was right in his own eyes.

commentary.text: The Israelites lament for the Benjamites.

—Israel lamented for the Benjamites, and were perplexed by the oath they had taken, not to give their daughters to them in marriage. Men are more zealous to support their own authority than that of God. They would have acted better if they had repented of their rash oaths, brought sin-offerings, and sought forgiveness in the appointed way, rather than attempt to avoid the guilt of perjury by actions quite as wrong. That men can advise others to acts of treachery or violence, out of a sense of duty, forms a strong proof of the blindness of the human mind when left to itself, and of the fatal effects of a conscience under ignorance and error.
